content.text: Imagine a world without friction. You would not be able to walk, write, or even pick up a glass of water. Cars could not brake, nails would slide out of walls, and every surface would be as slippery as ice. Friction is one of the most familiar forces in everyday life, yet it is often misunderstood.

that opposes the relative motion (or attempted motion) between two surfaces. In this lesson, we will explore the different types of friction, understand the factors that affect frictional forces, investigate drag and air resistance, explain how objects reach terminal velocity, and examine how friction can be both useful and harmful. These concepts connect directly to Newton's laws from the previous lesson and are essential for understanding motion in the real world.
is a force that opposes the motion (or the tendency to move) of an object across a surface. It acts at the boundary between two surfaces that are in contact.

At a microscopic level, even surfaces that appear smooth have tiny bumps and irregularities. When two surfaces are pressed together, these irregularities interlock, and forces of attraction act between the atoms of the two surfaces. These interactions resist sliding and produce the macroscopic effect we call friction.

There are two types of friction between solid surfaces:

is the friction that acts on a stationary object to prevent it from starting to move. If you push gently on a heavy box and it does not move, static friction is exactly matching your applied force. As you push harder, static friction increases — up to a maximum value. Once the applied force exceeds this maximum, the object starts to move.

At IGCSE level, you need to know that friction between two surfaces depends on:
Rougher surfaces produce more friction because the surface irregularities are larger and interlock more strongly. Smooth, polished surfaces have less friction.
The force pressing the surfaces together (normal contact force):
The harder the surfaces are pushed together, the more the irregularities interlock, and the greater the friction. For example, a heavier box on the same floor experiences more friction.
Different combinations of materials produce different amounts of friction. Rubber on concrete has high friction; steel on ice has very low friction.
The surface area in contact does

significantly affect friction for solid surfaces (at IGCSE level). This may seem surprising, but a larger contact area means the force is spread over more area, so the pressure at each point is lower, and the effects balance out.
is the resistive force experienced by an object moving through a fluid (a liquid or a gas).
is the specific name for drag in air.
Drag is a type of friction — it opposes the motion of the object through the fluid.
The faster the object moves, the greater the drag force. At higher speeds, the object collides with more fluid particles per second, and each collision transfers more momentum.

A larger area facing the direction of motion means the object pushes against more fluid, increasing drag. This is why a parachute (large area) experiences much more air resistance than a skydiver in freefall position.
shapes experience less drag than flat or irregular shapes. A streamlined shape allows the fluid to flow smoothly around the object with minimal turbulence.
Denser fluids produce more drag. Moving through water produces far more drag than moving through air because water is approximately 800 times denser.
is the constant maximum velocity reached by an object falling through a fluid when the drag force becomes equal to the weight of the object.

is the shaping of an object to reduce drag. A streamlined shape allows the fluid to flow smoothly around the object, reducing turbulence and therefore reducing the drag force.
Modern vehicles have curved, smooth shapes to reduce air resistance at high speeds, which improves fuel efficiency.
Wings and fuselages are carefully shaped to minimise drag.
Racing cyclists wear tight clothing and aerodynamic helmets, and adopt a crouched position to reduce their cross-sectional area and present a smoother shape to the air.
Their bodies have evolved streamlined shapes for efficient movement through water.
High-speed trains have pointed nose cones to reduce air resistance.
Friction is not simply "good" or "bad" — it is essential in many situations and harmful in others.
Friction between shoe soles and the ground provides grip. Without it, you would slip with every step (as on ice).
Friction between brake pads and the wheel disc (or drum) slows vehicles. This is essential for road safety.
Friction between a pen and paper allows ink to transfer.
Friction allows us to hold objects, turn handles, and use tools.
The friction between tyres and the road surface allows cars to accelerate, steer, and stop. Tyre treads are designed to channel water away and maintain contact with the road in wet conditions.
Friction generates heat when a match head is struck against the rough surface of the matchbox.
Friction between moving parts in engines and machines causes surfaces to wear away over time, reducing the lifespan of components.
Friction converts kinetic energy into thermal energy (heat). In machines, this represents wasted energy — the machine becomes less efficient.
Excessive friction can cause components to overheat. Bearings, axles, and gears can be damaged if friction generates too much heat.
Reducing friction where it is harmful:
Oil, grease, or other lubricants are applied between moving surfaces. The lubricant fills the gaps between surface irregularities and allows the surfaces to slide more easily.
These replace sliding friction with rolling friction, which is much smaller.
Polishing surfaces reduces the size of irregularities.
Hovercrafts ride on a cushion of air, virtually eliminating friction with the surface below.
Increasing friction where it is useful:
Sandpaper, textured floors, and grip tape increase friction.
Tyre treads, shoe soles, and sports equipment are designed with patterns that increase grip.
Football boots, running shoes, and climbing equipment use spikes or studs to increase friction on specific surfaces.

Example 6: Comparing Drag in Different Fluids
A metal sphere is dropped first through air and then through water. In both cases it reaches terminal velocity. Explain why the terminal velocity is lower in water than in air.

Water is much denser than air, so the drag force in water is much greater than in air at the same speed. The sphere reaches terminal velocity when drag equals weight. Because drag is larger in water at any given speed, the speed at which drag equals weight is reached at a much lower velocity. Therefore the terminal velocity in water is lower than in air.

(a) State the friction force acting on the block. (b) Explain how you know.

of relative motion between two surfaces. For a stationary object, static friction prevents it from sliding. Importantly, friction can act in the direction of motion — for example, when you walk, friction acts
on your foot. Without friction, your foot would slip backward and you could not walk. Friction opposes the backward slide of your foot, not your forward motion.

For solid surfaces at IGCSE level, the friction force does not depend on the contact area. A brick lying flat on a table experiences the same friction as the same brick standing on its end, despite the different contact areas. This is because a smaller area has greater pressure, which compensates for the reduced contact.
"Objects always slow down because of friction."
Friction converts kinetic energy to thermal energy, which can slow objects down. However, friction can also
— a car accelerates because of friction between the tyres and the road. Without friction, the wheels would spin on the spot.
"Heavier objects reach higher terminal velocities because gravity pulls them harder."

This is not always true and oversimplifies the situation. Terminal velocity depends on both weight and the drag characteristics (shape, cross-sectional area). A flat sheet of paper is heavier than a small lead ball bearing, but the paper has a much lower terminal velocity because it has a much larger cross-sectional area relative to its weight.
"At terminal velocity, there are no forces acting on the object."
At terminal velocity, forces still act — weight pulls the object downward and drag pushes upward. However, these forces are
force is zero. It is the resultant force that is zero, not the individual forces.

Air resistance changes with speed. The faster an object moves, the greater the air resistance. This is the key reason why terminal velocity is reached — air resistance increases until it matches the weight.

Friction is essential for walking, braking, writing, gripping objects, and many other everyday activities. Without friction, controlled movement would be impossible. Friction is only a disadvantage when it causes unwanted energy loss, wear, or overheating.

Friction is a force that opposes the motion (or the tendency to move) of an object across a surface in contact with another surface.

Static friction acts on a stationary object and prevents it from starting to move. It can vary from zero up to a maximum value. Kinetic friction acts on an object that is already sliding across a surface. It has a roughly constant value that is generally less than the maximum static friction.

(i) The roughness of the surfaces — rougher surfaces produce more friction. (ii) The force pressing the surfaces together (normal force) — a greater normal force produces more friction. (iii) The materials in contact — different pairs of materials produce different amounts of friction.

(a) The driving force is 900 N. (b) The car travels at constant speed in a straight line, so the acceleration is zero. By Newton's first law, the resultant force must be zero. Therefore the driving force must equal the total resistive force:

At higher speeds, air resistance is greater because drag increases with speed. The engine must provide a larger driving force to overcome this greater air resistance and maintain a constant speed. A larger driving force requires more fuel to be burned per second, so fuel consumption increases.

When the skydiver first jumps, their speed is zero and air resistance is negligible. Weight is much greater than air resistance, so there is a large resultant downward force. The skydiver accelerates rapidly. As speed increases, air resistance increases. The resultant downward force decreases, so the acceleration decreases (the skydiver is still speeding up, but at a decreasing rate). Eventually, air resistance equals weight, the resultant force is zero, and the skydiver falls at a constant terminal velocity. When the parachute opens, the cross-sectional area increases dramatically, causing a sudden large increase in air resistance. Air resistance is now much greater than weight, so the resultant force is upward. The skydiver decelerates. As speed decreases, air resistance decreases. Eventually, air resistance equals weight again at a new, much lower terminal velocity. The skydiver descends at this lower speed to land safely.

The golf ball is much heavier (larger weight) than the table tennis ball, but both have similar diameters and therefore similar cross-sectional areas. Terminal velocity is reached when drag equals weight. Since the golf ball has a greater weight, a greater drag force is needed to balance it. Since drag increases with speed, the golf ball must reach a higher speed before drag equals its weight. Therefore the golf ball has a higher terminal velocity.

Water on the brake pads and wheel rims acts as a lubricant, reducing the friction between the brake pads and the wheel. With reduced friction, the braking force is smaller, so the car takes longer to slow down and the stopping distance increases. Wet road surfaces also reduce the friction between the tyres and the road, making skidding more likely.

Useful: (i) Friction between tyres and the road allows cars to accelerate, steer, and brake safely. (ii) Friction between shoes and the ground provides grip for walking. Harmful: (i) Friction between moving parts in an engine causes wear and tear, reducing the lifespan of components. (ii) Friction converts kinetic energy to thermal energy, wasting energy and reducing the efficiency of machines.

The swimmer moves at constant velocity, so the acceleration is zero. By Newton's first law, the resultant force is zero. This means the forward thrust from the swimmer's strokes is exactly equal in magnitude to the backward drag force from the water. The forces are balanced.

Both sheets have the same mass and therefore the same weight. However, the flat sheet has a much larger cross-sectional area facing the direction of fall. This means it experiences much greater air resistance at any given speed. The flat sheet therefore reaches terminal velocity at a much lower speed. The crumpled sheet, with its smaller cross-sectional area, experiences less air resistance and reaches a higher terminal velocity. Therefore the crumpled sheet falls faster.

(i) Lubrication — applying oil or grease between moving parts reduces friction by filling in surface irregularities and allowing surfaces to slide more easily. (ii) Using ball bearings or roller bearings — these replace sliding friction with rolling friction, which is much smaller. Reducing friction is important because it reduces energy wasted as heat, reduces wear on components, prevents overheating, and increases the efficiency and lifespan of the machine.
